hints: Recall the Doppler effect for sound: a source moving towards a stationary observer compresses wavefronts so observed wavelength decreases and observed frequency is constant and greater than $f_S$ while approaching, and constant and less than $f_S$ while receding.
teacher_walkthrough: Doppler effect for a source moving at constant speed relative to a stationary observer gives a constant observed frequency shift while the velocity component towards the observer is constant.

For $0 \le t < t_1$ the train approaches at constant high speed, so $$f_o = f_S \frac{v}{v - v_S} > f_S$$ and is constant. Draw a horizontal line above the $f_S$ dashed line from $t = 0$ to $t = t_1$.
For $t_1 < t \le t_2$ the train recedes at constant speed, so $$f_o = f_S \frac{v}{v + v_S} < f_S$$ and is constant. Draw a horizontal line below the $f_S$ dashed line from $t = t_1$ to $t = t_2$.
The change occurs at $t = t_1$ when passing occurs, so show a vertical drop at $t_1$ between the two horizontal levels.
walkthrough: A1: horizontal line above $f_S$ from $t=0$ to $t=t_1$ and horizontal line below $f_S$ from $t=t_1$ to $t=t_2$ with step down at $t_1$.
common_pitfalls: Drawing a continuously decreasing sloping line through $t_1$ instead of two constant levels with a sudden drop, confusing transit Doppler shift with gradual change.
Drawing one or both lines at $f_S$ level, forgetting approaching gives higher frequency and receding gives lower frequency.
Showing frequency varying with distance while approaching or receding, forgetting speed is constant so Doppler shift is constant.

hints: Recall definition of wave intensity as power per unit area normal to propagation: $I = P/A$, so rearrange to $P = I \times A$.
Calculate the area of the circular detector with $A = \pi r^2$ after converting radius from cm to m: $r = 2.8 \text{ cm} = 0.028 \text{ m}$.
Substitute $I = 4.7 \times 10^{-3} \text{ Wm}^{-2}$ and your area in $\text{m}^2$ into $P = I A$ and evaluate to 2 significant figures in W.
teacher_walkthrough: Intensity is power per unit area for waves incident normally: $$I = \frac{P}{A}$$ so $$P = I A$$.
Area of circular detector is $$A = \pi r^2$$.
walkthrough: C1: use $I = P/A$ rearranged to $P = IA$.
common_pitfalls: Forgetting to convert radius from cm to m and using $r = 2.8$ in $\pi r^2$, giving area $24.6 \text{ m}^2$ and a power too large by factor $10^4$.
Using diameter instead of radius or using $2\pi r$ or $\pi d^2$, giving incorrect detector area.
Dividing intensity by area ($P = I/A$) instead of multiplying, confusing the definition $I = P/A$.
